extracted.intended_audience: general readers of early-20th-century progressive/feminist essays and fiction; socially conscious women and reformers
extracted.subtask_description: A mixed collection of short fiction, poems, social-critique essays and reviews addressing domestic life, gender roles, beauty, crime & punishment, and social reform in the early 20th century. Combines prescriptive social commentary with illustrative anecdote and artistic pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing the eye as well as the palate
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very important to please the eye as well as the palate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The host arranges a dainty, attractive service (silver-plated/aluminum dishes, neat presentation) so that the meal is enjoyed 'just as if I was a guest.' Aesthetic presentation is presented as integral to domestic hospitality and home attractiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meals should be hot and tempting
rubrics_metrics.description: Food must be hot and tempting; the sensory quality of food (temperature, taste, texture) matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soup 'hot', salad 'crisp', ice cream 'hard', sponge cake 'thick, light', coffee 'perfect and almost burned the tongue.' Delivered meals can match or exceed home-cooked standards when properly prepared and insulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical design constraints govern service choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical factors (weight, breakage, convenience) justify material and design choices in serviceware and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of aluminum/plated ware is defended because glass and silver are heavy and breakable; service design balances aesthetics with functional considerations like weight for delivery and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact, orderly service packaging and design
rubrics_metrics.description: Good meal-delivery/service systems should be neatly organized with secure fittings and compartments so nothing rattles or spills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described features: asbestos-lined compartments for heat/cold, perfectly fitting places for each dish, special drawer for small leavings, knives/forks held by rubber fittings, all items put back out of sight for collection—these design details preserve quality and appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty must belong to its subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is associative and must be appropriate to its subject; abstract 'beauty' varies with the kind of thing being judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that the same form/color may be beautiful in one context and disgusting in another (e.g., an iridescent shell vs. ancient meat). One should judge beauty relative to what is being considered (horse vs. bird vs. human).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate women's beauty as human/race beauty, not solely male sexual viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Women's beauty has been narrowed by measurement only from a masculine sexual viewpoint; it should be appraised as human or race beauty beyond mere sex-attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges expanding appreciation beyond costume, ornament, and sexual coquettishness to include proportions, strength, health, dignity, and broader human expression. Critiques female beauty valued only for attracting males and calls for recognition of full human beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative size and strength are elements of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative size and strength contribute to beauty; neither extreme dwarfism nor gigantism is beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes historical dwarfing of women via restricting conditions and suggests that as societies change, differences in size should diminish; strength and proper proportion are preferable to extreme slenderness or weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength (not feeble delicacy) is compatible with true beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Weakness in a healthy adult is incompatible with true 'race' beauty; beauty requires firm, vigorous, well-proportioned bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anecdote: a girl declines gymnasium for fear of big hands, showing misplaced vanity; author promotes gym training and strong muscles as components of beauty (smooth neck, firm trunk, active limbs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty derives from wide life experience and expressive range
rubrics_metrics.description: True beauty includes expressive depth that comes from a rich, wide life and active experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A woman's limited domestic range produces a 'puffy negation' in faces; beauty tied solely to maternal expression is incomplete. A face that shows the range of human life is more truly beautiful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask 'Why?' before punishing—seek causes of antisocial acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The first question of a rational mind confronted with offending conduct is 'Why?'—understand causes rather than immediately punish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes studying the conditions that produce conduct (social, economic, developmental) and argues that rational responses should address causes (e.g., poverty, bad rearing) rather than reflexive retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment based on retaliation is ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: The prehistoric base of punishment—retaliation—does not reduce crime proportionally to severity; escalating retaliation fails to stop crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical abuses (imprisonment, mutilation, torture, razing cities) did not proportionally reduce crime. Modern shifts aim toward reform rather than inflicting extreme punitive measures; the text criticizes the persistence of retaliatory instincts in child-rearing and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: An intelligent society prevents crime via child welfare and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Society should prevent crime by curing or treating moral disease and by removing the adverse conditions that produce offenders, especially in childhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed measures: hospitals for moral incurables, cure/treatment for some, and addressing poor conditions of birth and rearing (ill-fed, ill-dressed, ill-taught children) to prevent future criminals—i.e., prevention and care instead of mere punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural/collective remedies needed for new large-scale crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: For modern large-scale harms (polluting water/air, poisonous food, destructive tenement housing, press lies, trafficking), personal punitive responses are inadequate; structural prevention and regulation are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author enumerates crimes lacking adequate names/penalties (lying press, poisoning unborn children, pollution, exploiting women) and argues that stopping systemic processes (e.g., regulation, social reform) is more effective than pursuing individual punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective political/suffrage papers emphasize organized action and record
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffrage and movement newspapers are most effective when they focus on the record of work planned and done and act as secure party organs rather than spaces for argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: English suffrage papers ('Votes for Women', 'The Common Cause') are praised for being 'filled with the record of work planned and done' and for masterly leadership; American papers still give much space to argument and appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good life-story/biography
rubrics_metrics.description: A compelling life-story is vivid, interesting, readable, talks and laughs and lives, and 'reveals' rather than being a mere confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review of Alexander Irvine's 'From the Bottom Up' praises its liveliness, revelation of character, and usefulness in showing how 'the other half live'—implying biography should both move and inform readers.
